title: Climbing Himlung Himal: Full Guide
excerpt: Himlung Himal, 7,126 m in Nepal, is among the best peaks for a first climb above 7,000 m. The full guide: the Nar Phu valley, the camps, gear, oxygen, permits, season and cost.
seoTitle: Climbing Himlung Himal: Your First 7,000 m Peak, Route and Cost

content.value: On day 22 of the expedition, after almost two weeks of rotations between the high camps, climbers set out for the summit of Himlung Himal, 7,126 m (23,379 ft), and descend the same day to Camp 2. Himlung is a peak in the remote Nar Phu valley in northern Nepal, near the Tibetan border, in the region between Manaslu and Annapurna, and it is considered one of the best peaks in the world for a first climb above 7,000 m. The climb requires good fitness, previous mountaineering experience and adaptation to altitude, and on the way to the summit you cross snow slopes and glaciers and climb on fixed ropes. With us it is a 30-day expedition that departs in October.

Anyone who has already stood on a summit above 6,000 m usually asks what comes next, and the gap between such a summit and a peak above 8,000 m is large: in altitude, in the length of the expedition and in its complexity. Himlung sits halfway along that road. It is a genuine mountaineering expedition, with a base camp, high camps, rotations and fixed ropes, at an altitude where the body learns what happens above 7,000 m. This guide explains how our expedition works day by day, what awaits in the Nar Phu valley and on the mountain, how acclimatization works, what gear you need, which permits are required and what the price includes.
A first peak above 7,000 m

Himlung Himal rises to 7,126 m in northern Nepal, on the Tibetan border, above the Nar Phu valley. The valley lies within the Annapurna Conservation Area, and Nepal classifies it as a restricted area, which you can enter only with a special permit and a licensed guide. Because of that, and because of the distance, relatively few trekkers reach it, and the way to the mountain passes through quiet valleys and villages of Tibetan character, far from the tourist trails.

Himlung is considered one of the best peaks for a first climb at 7,000 m for two reasons. The first is that its technical difficulty is moderate for its altitude: the route crosses moraines, glaciers and snow slopes, and the steep sections are protected with fixed ropes. The second is that its structure is that of a major high-mountain expedition: a base camp, high camps, acclimatization rotations and a long summit day. Anyone who goes through all of this on Himlung learns the method on which expeditions to peaks above 8,000 m are also built.

content.value: The itinerary has three parts. In the first nine days you travel from Kathmandu to base camp, with an acclimatization day in Phu Gaun. The 12 days that follow, days 10 to 21, are set aside for rotations and acclimatization on the mountain, and day 22 is summit day. In the last part you descend the same way back to Kathmandu, with one spare day left before the flight home.

content.value: In our itinerary 12 days, days 10 to 21, are set aside for rotations and acclimatization between base camp and the high camps, before summit day. That time is what allows the body to adapt to the altitude before the final climb.
The way in: the Nar Phu valley

The first two days after Kathmandu are spent on the way to Koto, 2,600 m, via Besisahar in the Marsyangdi river valley. Jeep transfers from Kathmandu to the start of the trek and back are included in the price. As far as Koto this is also the road of the Annapurna Circuit, and at Koto, near Chame, the trail to the Nar Phu valley leaves it: you cross a suspension bridge and enter a narrow, forested gorge that climbs north.

From here the landscape changes quickly. From Koto you climb to the village of Meta, 3,560 m, almost 1,000 m of gain in sleeping altitude in a single day, and continue to Kyang and Phu Gaun. As you go on, the forests give way to a dry, high landscape of rock and deep gorges, and the villages take on a Tibetan character: stone houses, chortens, prayer flags and old monasteries. In Phu Gaun you stay an extra day to acclimatize, and the next day you climb to base camp, 4,900 m.

Along the trek you sleep in teahouses, the lodges of Nepal, in twin rooms, and in a remote valley like Nar Phu they are simpler than on the well-known routes. Three meals a day, chosen from the menu, are included throughout the climb. Porters carry your personal gear, up to 15 kg per person. Internet, laundry and extra meals at the teahouses are not included, so bring some cash for them.
We have written a complete guide to the road from Besisahar along the Marsyangdi valley, and to the whole Annapurna Circuit.

content.value: On the mountain: camps and rotations

Above base camp the Himlung route usually passes through three high camps. The exact altitudes vary slightly from one expedition to the next, and some teams skip the third camp and go for the summit from Camp 2. In our itinerary days 10 to 21 are set aside for rotations between the camps, and after the summit you descend to sleep at Camp 2.
Base camp and Camp 1

Base camp sits at about 4,900 m, and there and at the high camps you sleep in twin tents. On the way to Camp 1, at about 5,450 m, you cross a glacier and fields of moraine, and climb a steep moraine wall that already has fixed ropes on it.
Up to Camp 2

From Camp 1 you climb along fixed ropes to the shoulder of the mountain, and from there over the glacier to Camp 2, a little above 6,000 m. Here working with the jumar becomes routine: an ascender that locks onto the rope and is clipped to your harness, letting you move safely on a steep slope while your crampons bite into hard, frozen snow.
The wall, Camp 3 and the summit

Between Camp 2 and Camp 3, at about 6,400 m, lies the steepest section of the route: a traverse and a short ice wall climbed on a fixed rope. Above Camp 3 you continue on slopes of snow and ice, some of them steep, to the summit. Summit day starts in the dark and lasts many hours, and it is the most demanding day of the expedition. In our itinerary you descend at the end of it to Camp 2, so that you already sleep lower on the night after the summit.

content.value: Acclimatization: why altitude sets the pace

At 7,000 m every breath brings in less than half the oxygen it brings in at sea level, so the main danger on Himlung is the altitude, not the technical difficulty. Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness and fatigue. In serious cases it can develop into high altitude pulmonary or cerebral edema. When the symptoms get worse, you descend.

Rotations are the way to deal with this. Instead of going straight up, you climb to a high camp, sometimes carrying gear, and descend to sleep lower. Then you climb again, higher and for nights at the camps. That way the body gradually meets altitudes of 5,500 and 6,000 m before summit day. This is the principle of "climb high, sleep low", and it is what fills the 12 days between reaching base camp and summit day.

The way to base camp is part of acclimatization too: a week of gradual ascent from Kathmandu, through the Nar Phu valley, with an acclimatization day in Phu Gaun. Every group has a pulse oximeter and a Magnus satellite device, and every climber has a personal Sherpa guide, on a 1:1 ratio, who accompanies them to the summit. In the mountains there is no promise of a summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
Technical gear, ropes and oxygen

Himlung is not complex rock or ice climbing, but it is mountaineering in every sense. On the way to the summit you cross glaciers and snow slopes, and on the steep sections you climb on fixed ropes. Fixing the ropes along the route to the summit is included in the price of our expedition. On snow and ice you walk with crampons and an ice axe, and on the fixed ropes you climb with a harness and a jumar.

Personal gear, including clothing, footwear and climbing equipment, is not included in the price. The most important items are high-altitude mountaineering boots that take crampons and warm down clothing for the coldest days. Every registered climber receives a detailed gear list from us, and before departure you get a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.

And what about oxygen? On Himlung some climbers reach the summit without supplemental oxygen, and some use it on the upper part of the mountain. Supplemental oxygen does not appear in the list of what our expedition price includes, so anyone considering it should check with us before registering.
Permits, visa and insurance

The Nar Phu valley is a restricted area. To enter it you need a special permit, issued only through a registered trekking agency in Nepal, and you may enter only with a licensed guide. In addition you need an entry permit for the Annapurna Conservation Area and a climbing permit for the mountain itself. Permit prices depend on the season and on the length of the stay in the area. The Himlung climbing permit and all trek entry permits are included in the price of our expedition.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. The expedition spends 30 days in Nepal, every day of a 30-day visa, with no margin for weather days on the mountain, so you need a 90-day visa, which costs 125 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying a policy, check that it covers climbing to 7,126 m, including rescue and helicopter evacuation, and check your government's current travel advice for Nepal before you go.
When to go

Nepal has two main climbing seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. In the monsoon season, in the summer months, rain and cloud make the approach and the climb very difficult, and in winter the cold and the wind at 7,000 m are very harsh. Our Himlung expedition departs in October, after the end of the monsoon, when the skies are usually clearer. The spare day at the end of the itinerary is there in case the weather delays the way back.
Who it suits

Himlung is not a first peak. The climb requires good fitness, previous mountaineering experience and adaptation to altitude, but among 7,000 m peaks it is considered relatively accessible, and it suits climbers looking for a first taste of climbing at that altitude. We grade it extreme.

If you have not yet gained experience with crampons, an ice axe and a jumar on a fixed rope, it is worth doing so first. The natural route is a peak above 6,000 m in Nepal, such as Mera Peak or Island Peak, where you meet high altitude, a glacier and ropes on a much shorter expedition. That experience also teaches you how your body reacts to altitude, cold and long days.

content.value: A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join. The best preparation is months of endurance training, long uphill hikes with a heavy pack, and practice with ropes for those who need it.

Good to know: the climb is led by professional local guides who speak English, and a personal Sherpa guide walks beside every climber. Come with enough English to follow instructions in the field, on the ropes too. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides.
A step toward a peak above 8,000 m

For many climbers, Himlung is a stage on the way. Our Manaslu expedition, 8,163 m, the eighth highest mountain in the world, is meant for climbers who already have experience on 6,000 and 7,000 m peaks, and it is built on the same method: a trek through remote valleys to base camp, rotations between high camps, glaciers and fixed ropes on the way to the summit. It also lasts 30 days, and it departs in September.

Himlung lets you meet all of these elements about 1,000 m lower: living for weeks at a base camp and in tents, working with a jumar on fixed ropes at high altitude, and learning how your body reacts above 7,000 m. Anyone who comes back from Himlung healthy and eager for more knows far better whether they are ready for the next step.
What it costs and what is included

The Himlung expedition costs 8,500 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Kathmandu and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 4 nights in a 5-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms throughout the trek, double tents during the climb, dinners at a restaurant before and after the climb, three full meals a day throughout the climb, 2 liters of hot water a day, professional local English-speaking guides, a personal Sherpa guide all the way to the summit, fixed ropes along the route to the summit, porters for personal gear up to 15 kg per person, showers and toilets in the teahouses where available on the route, all entry permits for the trek and the climb, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, a pulse oximeter for the group, a Magnus satellite device for the group, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear (clothing, footwear, climbing gear and summit boots), tips for guides and porters (350 dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (800 dollars per person), a 90-day Nepal visa (125 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet.
Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.
Himlung with HighAir

At HighAir we go to Himlung in October, on a 30-day expedition, in groups of up to 10 climbers, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 80 percent. The itinerary gives the mountain the time it demands: a week of gradual ascent to base camp, 12 days of rotations and acclimatization, a summit day that ends with a descent to Camp 2, and a spare day at the end. And beside every climber, all the way to the summit, walks a personal Sherpa guide.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see on the highest summits in the world started once, on one mountain, and progressed from there step by step. If Himlung is your first peak above 7,000 m, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does it take to climb Himlung Himal?

The HighAir expedition lasts 30 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. Seven days are spent on the way from Kathmandu to base camp, including an acclimatization day in Phu Gaun, 12 days on rotations and acclimatization on the mountain, and day 22 is summit day. After it you descend to Kathmandu in six days, and there is one spare day for bad weather.
Do I need climbing experience to climb Himlung?

Yes. The climb requires good fitness, previous mountaineering experience and adaptation to altitude. On the way to the summit you cross glaciers and snow slopes and climb on fixed ropes, so it is worth arriving with experience of crampons, an ice axe and a jumar. Among 7,000 m peaks, Himlung is considered relatively accessible.
Is oxygen used when climbing Himlung?

Some climbers reach the summit of Himlung without supplemental oxygen, and some use it on the upper part of the mountain. Supplemental oxygen does not appear in the list of what our expedition price includes, and anyone considering it should check with us before registering.
Which permits do I need to climb Himlung?

The Nar Phu valley is a restricted area, which you can enter only with a special permit issued through a registered trekking agency in Nepal, and only with a licensed guide. In addition you need an entry permit for the Annapurna Conservation Area and a climbing permit for the mountain. The Himlung climbing permit and the trek entry permits are included in the price of our expedition. A 90-day Nepal visa, 125 US dollars, is not included.
When is the season for climbing Himlung?
The climbing seasons in Nepal are spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. Our Himlung expedition departs in October, after the end of the monsoon, when the skies are usually clearer.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by professional local guides who speak English, and every climber has a personal Sherpa guide who accompanies them to the summit.
